content.text: Mortgages are available in various formats, with 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate options being the most common. Loan terms can range from as short as five years to as long as 40 years or more. While extending the repayment period can lower monthly payments, it also significantly increases the total interest paid over the loan's duration. Types of mortgages Simple mortgage In a simple mortgage, the borrower pledges their property as security while retaining ownership. If the borrower defaults, the lender has the legal right to sell the property to recover dues, and any surplus from the sale goes to the borrower. Mortgage by conditional sale Here, the property's ownership is conditionally transferred to the lender. If the borrower repays the loan on time, the ownership remains theirs. However, in case of default, the transfer becomes effective. English mortgage The borrower transfers complete ownership of the property to the lender, with a promise to repay the loan on a specific date. Once the loan is fully repaid, ownership reverts to the borrower. Fixed-rate mortgage This mortgage features a constant interest rate throughout the loan tenure, providing stable and predictable monthly repayments, regardless of market fluctuations. Usufructuary mortgage In this arrangement, the borrower hands over possession of the property to the lender. The lender can use the property or earn rental income from it until the loan is repaid. Anomalous mortgage This is a non-standard mortgage that combines elements of different types or includes unique terms not covered by traditional mortgage categories. Reverse mortgage Designed for senior citizens, this allows homeowners to receive regular payments from a lender against the value of their home. Ownership remains with the borrower, and repayment is typically made by selling the property after the borrower's death or when they vacate the home. How Does a Mortgage Work? A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy a home, with the property serving as collateral. The borrower repays the loan in installments, typically monthly, which include principal (the loan amount) and interest. Mortgage terms usually last 15 or 30 years, with interest rates being either fixed or adjustable. If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender can foreclose on the property. Key factors like credit score, income, and debt-to-income ratio impact the loan approval process. Over time, as the mortgage is paid down, the borrower builds equity in the home. You don’t have to sell your home to access its value. Start by comparing interest rates—fixed versus variable—to understand potential cost fluctuations. Assess the loan tenure, as longer terms reduce monthly payments but increase total interest. Consider fees, including processing charges, prepayment penalties, and closing costs. Check the lender’s credibility and customer service quality. Use online calculators to compare monthly payments and overall costs. Additionally, review eligibility criteria, required documents, and flexibility in repayment options. Interest rates Compare the interest rates offered by different lenders. A lower rate can significantly reduce your overall loan cost. Loan tenure Assess the repayment period offered. A longer tenure can reduce your EMIs but may result in higher total interest payments. Processing fees and other charges Review the processing fees, administrative charges, and prepayment or foreclosure fees. These can vary significantly between lenders. Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio Check the LTV ratio, which determines the loan amount relative to the property value. A higher LTV means you can borrow more. Flexibility in repayment Look for loans with flexible repayment options, such as part-prepayment or EMI moratoriums, to ease financial stress. Eligibility criteria Ensure you meet the eligibility criteria for the mortgage, which may vary based on your income, credit score, and property type.
